## Edit / lint / format loop

After changing any `.ts` file, run in this order:

```bash
npm run typecheck
```

```bash
npm run lint
```

```bash
npm run format
```

- `npm run typecheck` runs `tsc --noEmit` to type-check `src`. Fix any
  reported type errors before continuing.
- `npm run lint` runs `oxlint` with its default rule set. Fix any

  files in place. Run it again after fixing lint errors, since edits
  can reintroduce formatting drift.
- Re-run `npm start` to confirm the code still runs correctly under
  Node's TS support after linting/formatting.

Repeat edit → typecheck → lint → format until `tsc` and `oxlint`
report no issues and `oxfmt` makes no further changes.

A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). content.text: I fixed the parser, but nothing is committed yet. **What broke:** In today's run, Step 3 failed when it tried to read the OpenCode Zen pricing page. That page now shows a sale price as `Mistral Large 4 (50% off)$1.36 $0.68…`. The parser read the crossed-out old price and the new price together as one value, `"$1.36 $0.68"`, and refused it. So the run kept yesterday's Zen pricing file and exited with code 1. Because of that, the mapping and data commits, the site build and the deploy were all skipped. Copilot, OpenCode Go and ClinePass pricing, the benchmark data and the scoring all finished fine. **Fix** in [src/opencode-zen/parser.ts](src/opencode-zen/parser.ts): - The parser now ignores crossed-out text (`` and `` tags) along with footnote markers, so a sale cell reads as the current price. - It removes a `(N% off)` suffix from the model name, so the model keeps the name `Mistral Large 4`. The discount is saved in `notes` as "Promotional pricing (50% off)." instead. I tested it on today's live page: all 103 rows parse, and Mistral Large 4 comes out at $0.68 input, $2.09 output and $0.07 cached read. Typecheck, lint and format all pass. I didn't run the full `npm start`, because it rewrites the files under `data/` and could start the local parser-repair agent. **Not causing the failure, but worth knowing:** - 47 models are skipped for "incomplete benchmark data", including the GPT 5 and 6 models and every Claude model. Only 75 candidates got scored. Benchmark data comes from Artificial Analysis on the free tier (`tier: free`), which may now leave some fields out. That's worth checking if the rankings look thin. - OpenCode Go has some "no matching row in: requests" warnings for the variants split by context length (GPT 6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5). Should I commit and push this so tomorrow's scheduled run picks it up, or would you rather start the workflow manually after pushing?

content.text:
The pipeline isn't dropping any data. Artificial Analysis (the benchmark source) simply hasn't published coding and agentic scores for these models yet, and our scorer skips any model that's missing a score.

**What I found** (34 benchmark entries behind the 47 skip messages, since several providers share entries):
- **25 of 34 have an intelligence score but no coding or agentic score.** That includes all the Claude and GPT 5.x/6 models, Grok 4.7, GLM 5, MiniMax M2.5 and MiMo v2.6.
- **5 are missing only agentic** (GPT 5, 5.1, 5.4, Qwen3.6 Plus, Kimi K2.5), **2 are missing only speed** (DeepSeek V4 Flash, LongCat 2.0), and **2 have nothing at all** (GPT 5.4 Pro, GPT 5.5 Pro).
- **This isn't new.** Every snapshot since September 17 has the same gaps, and no model has lost a score.
- **The free tier probably isn't the cause.** The feed includes coding and agentic scores for Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT 6 Astra, which are just as new and high-end. I can't fully confirm without a paid key, but the gaps look like models Artificial Analysis hasn't tested yet.
- **The gaps depend on the model's age:**
  - Older models were released before those scores existed. Only 12 of 186 models from before mid-2025 have them.
  - Brand-new models haven't been tested yet: Opus 5.5 (released Sep 22), Sonnet 5.5 (Sep 28), GPT 6.1 Sol (Sep 29), Haiku 5.5 (Oct 7).
  - Opus 5.5 is ranked first overall on intelligence, but we can't score it.

**Why the skip happens:** [compute-scores.ts:198-210](src/scoring/compute-scores.ts:198) requires every score to be present. All four categories give the agentic score some weight (from 5% in `codeReview` to 50% in `agenticCoding`), so a model without it is skipped everywhere.

**What I'd recommend:** keep the rule, but stop hiding the skipped models.
- Filling in made-up scores or spreading the weight over the other scores would rank frontier models on partial data. That would quietly favour or penalise exactly the models people care most about.
- Instead, I can add an "awaiting benchmarks" list to `recommendations.json` and the site. It would name the models we skipped and which score each is missing. The models then join the rankings on their own once Artificial Analysis publishes their scores, with no further work needed.

The other option is to score with whatever data a model has and spread the missing weight over the rest. Rankings would then include the new models right away, but each ranking would rest on different data, and I'd mark those entries as partial.

There's also a separate set of 14 "no Artificial Analysis mapping" skips (Gemini 3.x, GPT 5.4, Qwen3.8 Flash and others). Those may just need entries in `config/model-mapping.json`.

Should I build the "awaiting benchmarks" list, or would you rather have the partial scoring?

content.text:
I made the change: models that are missing some benchmark scores are now ranked, with each missing score counted as zero. I haven't committed it yet. When I ran scoring on today's data, the number of ranked models went from 75 to 118, but the recommendations stayed almost the same.

**What changed in [compute-scores.ts](src/scoring/compute-scores.ts):**
- A missing score adds nothing to the model's total. That puts it level with the lowest-scoring model that does have the score.
- The scale for each score is set only by the models that have it. If I stored missing scores as a real 0, the bottom of every scale would drop to 0 and everyone else's numbers would shift.
- Each scored model now lists the scores it's missing (`missingMetrics`). The breakdown shows those as null, which the site already displays as "–".
- Models with no benchmark data at all are still skipped, since they would be ranked on price alone. That's only GPT 5.4 Pro and GPT 5.5 Pro.
- The log now says "Partial benchmark data … scored as 0" for each of these models instead of "Skipping".

**What it does to the rankings:**
- None of the newly ranked models makes a top-2 list. The only changes are in `llmWiki`. On OpenCode Go, Qwen3.8 Max replaces DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp. On Zen, the same two models swap places, which comes from the price scale widening with more models, not from a new entry.
- Zeroing the agentic and coding scores pushes the newest frontier models near the bottom. On Copilot (27 models):

| Category | Claude Opus 5.5 | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| agenticCoding | 19th | 18th | 21st |
| codeReview | 16th | 17th | 19th |
| softwareFactory | 20th | 18th | 23rd |
| llmWiki | 15th | 14th | 17th |

Your coding-focused categories weight the agentic and coding scores at 50–70%, so a model missing both has almost no chance to rank well. In practice "zero when missing" means "listed, but ranked last until Artificial Analysis publishes its scores". That's fair if you want only proven models recommended. If you were hoping to see Opus 5.5 near the top now, this won't do it.
